entry.title: EU Finds Meta in Breach of Digital Services Act Over Failure to Protect Children Under 13
entry.summary: The European Commission preliminarily found Meta's Instagram and Facebook in breach of the Digital Services Act for failing to prevent children under 13 from accessing the platforms, potentially exposing the company to fines of up to 6 percent of its global annual turnover.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The European Commission preliminarily found Meta's Instagram and Facebook in breach of the Digital Services Act for failing to prevent children under 13 from accessing the platforms, potentially exposing the company to fines of up to 6 percent of its global annual turnover.

The Commission announced its preliminary findings on April 29, 2026, concluding Meta had "disregarded readily available scientific evidence" about children's vulnerability to social media harms. Despite Meta's terms of service setting the minimum age at 13, approximately 10 to 12 percent of EU children under 13 are using Instagram or Facebook—roughly one in ten—contradicting the company's own internal assessments. The core failure is structural: children can bypass Meta's age restrictions by entering a false birth date during sign-up, with no verification step, while the reporting mechanism for removing underage accounts is described by the Commission as cumbersome and often ineffective. Meta disputed the findings, stating that "Instagram and Facebook are intended for people aged 13 and older and we have measures in place to detect and remove accounts from anyone under that age." Under DSA rules, Meta now has the right to examine the investigation file, submit a written reply, and propose corrective measures before any formal non-compliance decision is issued.

Why it matters: A confirmed non-compliance decision under the DSA would expose Meta to fines of up to 6 percent of its total worldwide annual turnover—which at Meta's current revenue scale could reach several billion euros, ranking among the largest digital-regulation penalties in EU history. The DSA proceeding is structurally distinct from GDPR child-protection cases: the obligation under Article 34 is proactive systemic-risk mitigation, not simply age-gating, meaning Meta must design systems that functionally prevent under-13 access rather than merely prohibit it in terms of service. This is the Commission's first child-protection enforcement action under the DSA, and the outcome will signal how aggressively the EU pursues platform accountability for minor safety across all seven designated gatekeepers—Apple, Google, Amazon, ByteDance, and others will be watching. The US Senate simultaneously advanced child-online-safety legislation in May 2026, creating parallel regulatory pressure from two major jurisdictions. Meta's corrective-measures response will likely determine whether the Commission issues a formal penalty or accepts voluntary undertakings—a choice that will define the DSA's enforcement character for every major case that follows.

entry.title: Musk v. Altman Week 2: OpenAI Fires Back as Shivon Zilis Reveals Musk Tried to Recruit Altman to Tesla
entry.summary: As the $134 billion OpenAI trial entered its second week in Oakland, Shivon Zilis testified that Elon Musk attempted to recruit Sam Altman to lead a competing AI company at Tesla and asked researcher Andrej Karpathy to compile a list of top OpenAI employees to poach, while OpenAI countered that Musk is suing to destroy a commercial rival to xAI.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

As the $134 billion OpenAI trial entered its second week in Oakland, Shivon Zilis testified that Elon Musk attempted to recruit Sam Altman to lead a competing AI company at Tesla and asked researcher Andrej Karpathy to compile a list of top OpenAI employees to poach, while OpenAI countered that Musk is suing to destroy a commercial rival to xAI.

The trial, which began April 27, 2026 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, centers on whether OpenAI's transformation from a nonprofit into a capped-profit entity violated a charitable trust Musk helped found, with Musk seeking $134 billion in damages. OpenAI's week-two legal strategy turned sharply offensive: the company argued Musk had demanded majority equity and the CEO position in any for-profit structure, and sued only after those demands were refused. OpenAI president Greg Brockman testified that after cofounders proposed equal equity splits, Musk stormed out saying "I actually thought he was going to hit me." Shivon Zilis—a former OpenAI board member who later bore Musk's children through IVF and joined Tesla and Neuralink—testified that Musk attempted to recruit Altman to lead an AI lab at Tesla around 2017 and asked Andrej Karpathy "to send a list of top OpenAI people to poach." Musk's counsel Steven Molo cross-examined Brockman on his approximately $30 billion equity stake despite never investing personal funds and on his holdings in Cerebras, CoreWeave, and Helion Energy—all companies with existing OpenAI business relationships—arguing financial self-interest overshadowed mission fidelity.

Why it matters: Judge Gonzalez Rogers will issue the binding ruling after weighing the advisory jury's findings; a decision against OpenAI could delay or derail its planned IPO at approximately $1 trillion valuation, with direct consequences for Microsoft's $13 billion equity stake. The trial is producing an unusually detailed public record of AI governance: Musk's December 2017 pivot to building an AI lab at Tesla after concluding OpenAI was "unlikely to build AGI," his attempted poaching of Altman and other researchers, and the competing equity demands all illuminate how the competitive AI landscape took its current shape. Ilya Sutskever and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella are scheduled to testify in coming days—Nadella's appearance is significant because it may require him to explain publicly what consideration Microsoft provided for its equity stake, a question central to the nonprofit-breach theory. SpaceX is targeting a June 2026 IPO at a $1.75 trillion valuation, giving Musk financial incentives to manage the litigation's public impact carefully. The advisory jury's deliberations and verdict are expected within two weeks, after which Judge Gonzalez Rogers will set her own timeline for the final ruling.

entry.title: Iran Sends Formal Ceasefire Response via Pakistan, Insisting War Must End on All Fronts Before Nuclear Talks
entry.summary: Iran transmitted its formal response to the US ceasefire proposal through Pakistani mediators on May 10, demanding the war end on all fronts—including in Lebanon—before any nuclear discussions begin, a sequencing demand that directly contradicts Washington's insistence on denuclearization first.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Iran transmitted its formal response to the US ceasefire proposal through Pakistani mediators on May 10, demanding the war end on all fronts—including in Lebanon—before any nuclear discussions begin, a sequencing demand that directly contradicts Washington's insistence on denuclearization first.

The US 14-point proposal required Iran to halt uranium enrichment for at least 12 years, surrender approximately 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent, agree not to develop nuclear weapons, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, in exchange for gradual sanctions relief, the release of billions in frozen Iranian assets, and withdrawal of the US naval blockade. Iran's counterproposal, transmitted exclusively through Pakistan—the sole recognized mediation channel—rejects the nuclear timeline as non-negotiable and makes any deal conditional on a comprehensive end to hostilities that includes Lebanon, where Hezbollah continues to fight. Iranian Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf stated publicly that a "full ceasefire could only work if the US naval blockade is lifted first." Analyst Abbas Aslani of the Center for Middle East Strategic Studies described Iran's response as "not a yes or no but a clarification of Iranian views," suggesting negotiations are continuing rather than collapsing. A nominal ceasefire has been in place since April 8, 2026, but both sides traded fire in the Strait of Hormuz on May 8, and a drone struck a vessel near Qatar on May 10 as Iran's IRGC warned the US against attacking its ships.

Why it matters: The sequencing dispute—denuclearize first versus stop fighting first—is the structural barrier that prior US-Iran negotiations, including the 2015 JCPOA process, never faced in this acute form because those talks occurred without an active, multi-front war underway. Pakistan's singular role as the sole intermediary creates fragile diplomatic architecture: no European government, UN body, or Gulf state holds an equivalent mediation channel, meaning any change in Pakistani domestic politics or foreign policy could strand negotiations instantly. The Strait of Hormuz closure is constraining roughly 20 percent of global LNG exports and depressing oil supply to Asian markets—Japan, South Korea, India—whose governments have no formal vote in the negotiation and face growing domestic economic pressure from the disruption. President Trump's declared red line against Iranian enrichment means accepting Iran's current counterproposal would require a public reversal of a stated presidential commitment, manageable only through creative face-saving language that neither side has yet offered. The Lebanon variable is the hidden complication with no obvious bridging formula: Iran insists on treating Lebanon and Iran as a single front requiring unified resolution, while Washington has consistently treated them as separate diplomatic tracks that can and should be decoupled.

entry.title: The Nine Lives of Employment Division v. Smith
entry.summary: A new SCOTUSblog analysis traces how the Supreme Court has spent thirty-five years systematically narrowing Employment Division v. Smith without overruling it—hollowing out the 1990 free-exercise precedent through successive rulings that have left it technically intact but practically enfeebled.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A new SCOTUSblog analysis traces how the Supreme Court has spent thirty-five years systematically narrowing Employment Division v. Smith without overruling it—hollowing out the 1990 free-exercise precedent through successive rulings that have left it technically intact but practically enfeebled.

Employment Division v. Smith (1990), written by Justice Antonin Scalia, held that the First Amendment's Free Exercise Clause provides no exemption from neutral, generally applicable laws—even when those laws substantially burden religious practice—and upheld Oregon's uniform drug prohibition as applied to peyote used in Native American Church ceremonies. Congress responded with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 (RFRA), restoring a compelling-interest test for federal laws, but the Court in 1997 limited RFRA to federal rather than state government actions. Rather than overruling Smith, the Court has pursued doctrinal erosion: Tandon v. Newsom (2021) held that strict scrutiny applies whenever a law treats "any comparable secular activity" more favorably than religious exercise, and Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021) established that any law containing any exception at all cannot qualify as "generally applicable." Three justices—Alito, Thomas, and Gorsuch—have publicly called Smith "regrettable" and urged overruling; Justices Barrett and Kavanaugh have expressed skepticism about the precedent but acknowledged that overruling requires an agreed-upon replacement framework that a five-justice majority has not yet coalesced around.

Why it matters: The "nine lives" framing captures the Court's institutional ambivalence: a near-majority appears to believe Smith was wrongly decided, but the inability to agree on a replacement standard has preserved a precedent being steadily drained of content through qualification. The practical consequence for state and local governments is substantial uncertainty: under Tandon and Fulton, any regulatory scheme containing any exception or accommodation—however minor or unrelated to religion—may now face strict scrutiny from religious claimants, chilling otherwise lawful regulation across healthcare, licensing, and non-discrimination law. Democratic proposals to narrow RFRA—specifically by excluding federal healthcare and LGBTQ non-discrimination obligations from its protection—could force the Court's hand by presenting cases where RFRA itself is the battleground rather than a state law, removing the Court's ability to resolve cases on narrower grounds. The 21 states with their own RFRA analogs have independent trajectories, meaning even a definitive Supreme Court ruling on federal doctrine would leave state-level religious exemption law evolving separately. The next case presenting a genuinely neutral and universally applicable law with no exceptions whatsoever would force a direct confrontation with Smith that the Court has artfully avoided for three decades.

entry.title: FBI Raids Office of Virginia Democratic Leader Who Championed 10-1 Democratic Redistricting Maps, With Fox News Pre-Positioned at the Scene
entry.summary: FBI agents raided the Portsmouth home office of Virginia Democratic State Senate leader L. Louise Lucas—the legislator whose redistricting effort produced a 10-1 Democratic congressional advantage ratified by voters in April—with Fox News already positioned at the scene before the search began, raising questions about law enforcement-media coordination.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

FBI agents raided the Portsmouth home office of Virginia Democratic State Senate leader L. Louise Lucas—the legislator whose redistricting effort produced a 10-1 Democratic congressional advantage ratified by voters in April—with Fox News already positioned at the scene before the search began, raising questions about law enforcement-media coordination.

Louise Lucas was the central Democratic figure in Virginia's 2026 redistricting initiative, a Democrat-led effort to redraw the state's congressional district boundaries in response to prior Republican gerrymandering. Virginia voters approved the new maps via referendum in April 2026, shifting the congressional delegation from a 6-5 Democratic advantage to a projected 10-1 Democratic majority—a dramatic reversal that prompted Trump to label the outcome a "RIGGED ELECTION" on Truth Social and Lucas to respond to Senator Ted Cruz's criticism with "You all started it and we fucking finished it." FBI agents searched Lucas's Portsmouth office on May 8, 2026; according to anonymous sources cited by the Associated Press and New York Times, the investigation concerned corruption allegations that opened during the Biden administration, predating the redistricting controversy. Fox News reporter Alex Hogan—previously listed as a London-based correspondent—was already present at the search site before agents arrived; Fox subsequently revised Hogan's biography page after scrutiny of this fact emerged. As of publication, no charges have been filed against Lucas and no court documents have been made public.

Why it matters: The most significant legal question is whether the FBI's apparent pre-coordination with Fox News before an unannounced search raises Fourth Amendment execution concerns and whether the timing—against a legislator whose redistricting maps the administration publicly denounced—creates a pattern that implicates First Amendment and equal-protection principles even if the stated underlying allegations are formally unrelated to redistricting. Fox's advance knowledge suggests someone in or with access to the investigative chain informed the outlet, conduct that, if proven, could affect the admissibility of evidence and expose participants to accountability under DOJ leak guidelines. Virginia's redistricting fight is itself a downstream consequence of the Supreme Court's 2019 Rucho v. Common Cause decision that partisan gerrymandering is a non-justiciable political question; states have since engaged in an unregulated partisan mapmaking competition with no federal judicial check. The raid joins a growing pattern of federal law enforcement actions against Democratic officials involved in electoral map challenges, which civil rights organizations say raises systemic rule-of-law concerns regardless of individual cases' legal merits. Lucas's defiant public posture signals that any eventual charges will be contested aggressively and framed as politically motivated prosecution, making the government's charging decision—and its timing—a significant political and legal event in its own right.

entry.title: DMA at Two: EU's Big Tech Law Produced Real Market Changes—but Compliance Theater Blunts Its Impact
entry.summary: Two years after the EU Digital Markets Act entered into force, analysis finds the regulation has produced tangible gains—a 500 million euro Apple fine, cross-platform messaging rights, measurable browser competition—but up to 66 percent of frequent users report that gatekeeper compliance increases friction rather than delivering the promised consumer benefits.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Two years after the EU Digital Markets Act entered into force, analysis finds the regulation has produced tangible gains—a 500 million euro Apple fine, cross-platform messaging rights, measurable browser competition—but up to 66 percent of frequent users report that gatekeeper compliance increases friction rather than delivering the promised consumer benefits.

The Digital Markets Act took effect in May 2023, designating seven platforms as "gatekeepers"—Apple, Google, Meta, Amazon, ByteDance, and two others—and imposing interoperability, data-sharing, and anti-steering obligations designed to open their ecosystems to competition. Concrete changes for EU consumers include the ability to set alternative browsers and payment apps as iPhone defaults, enforceable cross-platform messaging (a Latvian startup called BirdyChat now allows users to message WhatsApp contacts from outside Meta's ecosystem), and choice screens that have measurably shifted browser market share toward privacy-focused alternatives like Firefox. The Commission fined Apple 500 million euros in April 2025 for anti-steering violations that blocked App Store developers from directing users to cheaper purchases outside the App Store, and fined Meta 200 million euros for its "consent-or-pay" advertising model—both fines have been appealed. The Commission's April 2026 first formal DMA review declared the law "fit for purpose" while acknowledging a "ping-pong" enforcement dynamic: gatekeepers submit changes, the Commission requests improvements, and the cycle repeats without conclusive resolution. The Commission is now investigating Meta's integration of AI features into WhatsApp without a user opt-out, testing whether the DMA's systemic-risk provisions can reach AI-embedded features that post-date the regulation's drafting.

Why it matters: The DMA's two-year record reveals the gap between structural obligation and behavioral change: Apple and Meta have technically complied with most formal requirements while engineering compliance to increase friction and discourage users from exercising the rights the law creates—a pattern up to 66 percent of frequent users report experiencing as longer searches and less relevant results, and critics describe as "compliance theater." The 500 million euro Apple fine and 200 million euro Meta fine are significant but represent small fractions of both companies' annual revenues; credible deterrence requires the Commission to demonstrate willingness to escalate toward the DMA's ceiling of 10 percent of global annual turnover, a threshold that has not yet been invoked. The AI integration investigations are the most consequential test of the DMA's scope since enactment: if embedding AI features constitutes a new market-access barrier under Article 34 systemic-risk obligations, the regulation's reach will extend far beyond what the 2023 text explicitly anticipated and could require legislative clarification. The "fit for purpose" review signals no legislative revisions are imminent, meaning enforcement-through-fines remains the primary lever for at least two more years, making the size and sequencing of upcoming penalty decisions the decisive variable for the DMA's deterrence effect. Transatlantic tensions complicate enforcement: the Trump administration has signaled it views DMA actions targeting American companies as discriminatory trade policy, creating diplomatic pressure the Commission must navigate alongside its legal proceedings.

entry.title: Too Dangerous to Deploy: Anthropic’s Mythos and What Comes Next
entry.summary: Anthropic’s Mythos Preview — a frontier AI model that can autonomously exploit software vulnerabilities within hours of discovery — is the first AI system deemed too dangerous for public release, spurring the Trump administration to reverse course on AI oversight.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Anthropic’s Mythos Preview — a frontier AI model that can autonomously exploit software vulnerabilities within hours of discovery — is the first AI system deemed too dangerous for public release, spurring the Trump administration to reverse course on AI oversight.

On April 7, 2026, Anthropic announced Mythos Preview, a frontier AI model with hacking capabilities so potent the company declared it “too dangerous” for unrestricted public release. Mythos can autonomously identify and exploit previously unknown software vulnerabilities “potentially within minutes or hours of discovery” — capabilities that “surpass all but the most skilled human” operators, according to Anthropic. The company reported the model had already found thousands of high-severity vulnerabilities, including some in every major operating system and web browser. Rather than a standard commercial launch, Anthropic restricted access to approximately 50 industry partners — including Amazon, Apple, Cisco, Google, Microsoft, and NVIDIA — through Project Glasswing, a defensive cybersecurity initiative backed by $100 million in usage credits and $4 million in direct donations to non-profit security groups. The Pentagon had designated Anthropic a “supply chain risk” in March 2026, but Mythos’s capabilities prompted Dario Amodei to meet White House officials; Trump told CNBC afterward that a defense deal was “possible.” The Commerce Department’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation subsequently announced expanded pre-deployment testing agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft, and xAI.

Why it matters: Mythos marks the first instance of a major AI lab voluntarily restricting a commercial model’s release on capability-safety grounds rather than product readiness — a precedent the AI governance community has long advocated but never secured through voluntary commitments alone. The model’s autonomous vulnerability exploitation compresses the patch-response window from the current weeks-to-months standard to potentially hours, rendering current patch cadence fatally inadequate for under-resourced institutions like hospitals, schools, and utilities. The Trump administration’s shift from opposition to Biden-era AI oversight toward active model-testing frameworks signals that national security realities can override ideological hostility to regulation — but the resulting framework remains voluntary and fragmented, covering only companies that signed CAISI agreements. European allies were excluded from Glasswing’s 50 founding partners, intensifying transatlantic tensions over AI access and defensive coordination. The key question: whether Congress codifies any pre-deployment evaluation requirement, or whether Mythos remains a one-time exception that the next generation of AI companies is free to ignore.

entry.title: What we know about Iran’s response to the latest US ceasefire proposal
entry.summary: Iran submitted a 14-point counterproposal to Pakistani mediators on May 10 demanding a complete end to the war on all fronts, rejecting the US requirement to halt uranium enrichment for twelve years and insisting on UN Security Council guarantees against future attacks.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Iran submitted a 14-point counterproposal to Pakistani mediators on May 10 demanding a complete end to the war on all fronts, rejecting the US requirement to halt uranium enrichment for twelve years and insisting on UN Security Council guarantees against future attacks.

The United States’ 14-point proposal demanded that Iran cease uranium enrichment for at least 12 years, surrender approximately 440 kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent, agree not to develop nuclear weapons, and reopen the Strait of Hormuz — in exchange for gradual sanctions relief, the release of billions in frozen Iranian assets, and withdrawal of the US naval blockade within 30 days. Iran’s counterproposal, transmitted through Pakistan as the sole mediating channel, rejects the nuclear enrichment demand as non-negotiable and calls for UN Security Council guarantees against future attacks, complete sanctions lifting, war reparations, and a new maritime protocol for the Strait of Hormuz rather than simply reopening it. Iranian lawmaker Ebrahim Rezaei called the US proposal “more of an American wish-list than a reality,” while Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf publicly mocked the negotiations on social media. Despite ongoing diplomatic exchanges, both sides traded fire in the Strait of Hormuz on May 8, and a drone struck a vessel off Qatar on May 10 as Iran warned the US against attacking its ships.

Why it matters: The core division is structural, not cosmetic: Washington wants to denuclearize first and end hostilities second; Tehran wants to stop the war on all fronts — including Lebanon, where Hezbollah is still fighting — before any nuclear discussion, a sequencing disagreement that substantially narrows the negotiating space. Pakistan’s role as sole intermediary is itself a vulnerability: no European power, UN body, or Gulf state has been granted the same diplomatic channel, meaning any breakdown in Pakistani neutrality could collapse the talks entirely. The Strait of Hormuz closure continues to suppress global oil export volumes and disrupt supply chains across Asia and Europe; the longer it remains closed, the greater the pressure on both sides from third-party economies with no stake in the nuclear dispute. President Trump’s declared “red line” on enrichment means any deal permitting continued Iranian enrichment — which Tehran insists on — would require Trump to accept a public retreat from his stated position. The Lebanon question is the hidden complication: Iran’s counterproposal makes comprehensive war termination conditional on resolving Hezbollah’s ongoing conflict, which Washington has treated as a separate track — but Tehran refuses to separate them.

entry.title: But First, Implementation
entry.summary: Hungary’s new Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose Tisza party won a constitutional supermajority with 53% of the vote on May 9, demanded that President Tamás Sulyok and Chief Justice András Varga resign by May 31 or face removal, launching Hungary’s most consequential attempt at constitutional repair since Orbán’s 2010 consolidation.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Hungary’s new Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose Tisza party won a constitutional supermajority with 53% of the vote on May 9, demanded that President Tamás Sulyok and Chief Justice András Varga resign by May 31 or face removal, launching Hungary’s most consequential attempt at constitutional repair since Orbán’s 2010 consolidation.

Hungary’s 2026 parliamentary election saw Magyar’s Tisza party secure 53.1 percent of the vote, which under Hungary’s electoral system translated into a constitutional supermajority — enough seats to amend the constitution without coalition partners. Magyar was sworn in as prime minister in early May 2026, ending Viktor Orbán’s rule that began with a similar supermajority in 2010 and progressively restructured Hungary’s judiciary, prosecutorial service, and public broadcasting to entrench Fidesz authority. In his inaugural speech to the National Assembly, Magyar demanded President Tamás Sulyok — a Fidesz appointee — resign no later than May 31, and separately called on Chief Justice András Varga to do the same, calling both “puppets” of Orbán. Verfassungsblog’s analysis of the situation notes a central paradox: Tisza holds enough power to fix the constitution, but reversing Orbán’s changes while respecting European rule-of-law norms requires Magyar not to use the same majoritarian tools Orbán deployed. Hungary’s Constitutional Court, the Prosecutor General’s office, and the State Audit Office remain staffed by Fidesz-era appointees with fixed terms that cannot be easily shortened without constitutional changes Magyar has not yet formally proposed.

Why it matters: Hungary’s case is the sharpest live test of whether a post-autocratic government can dismantle illiberal institutions without replicating the constitutional shortcuts that built them — the same challenge Poland faced after its 2023 election, where the new government’s attempts to restore judicial independence triggered counter-challenges at the Constitutional Tribunal it was trying to reform. If Magyar removes Sulyok and Varga unilaterally, he risks creating the same type of executive-over-judiciary precedent that EU institutions condemned Orbán for establishing. If he waits for voluntary resignations that may never come, Fidesz-appointed officials retain enough institutional leverage — especially in the Constitutional Court — to block or delay his reform agenda. The EU’s rule-of-law conditionality framework, which froze approximately €30 billion in cohesion funds to Hungary during the Orbán era, is now watching whether Magyar’s government satisfies European Court of Justice standards in process as well as outcome. The May 31 deadline Magyar set is the first concrete test: Sulyok and Varga’s responses will signal whether the institutional transition will be negotiated or contested.

entry.title: The Dialectic of Viewpoint Discrimination
entry.summary: On the anniversary of Germany’s World War II surrender, the Bundesrat began debate on a Hesse-sponsored bill that would criminalize publicly denying Israel’s right to exist with up to five years in prison, reigniting a fundamental constitutional debate about whether Germany’s historical obligations can justify viewpoint-based speech restrictions.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

On the anniversary of Germany’s World War II surrender, the Bundesrat began debate on a Hesse-sponsored bill that would criminalize publicly denying Israel’s right to exist with up to five years in prison, reigniting a fundamental constitutional debate about whether Germany’s historical obligations can justify viewpoint-based speech restrictions.

The proposed legislation, introduced by the state of Hesse in the Bundesrat, would create a new criminal offence targeting anyone who “publicly or in an assembly denies the right of the State of Israel to exist or calls for the elimination of the State of Israel in a manner capable of encouraging antisemitic acts of violence or arbitrary measures.” Hesse frames the bill as closing a legal loophole not covered by Holocaust denial laws, with penalties of up to five years in prison or a fine. The top administrative court in North Rhine-Westphalia ruled in November 2025 that questioning Israel’s right to exist does not constitute an existing criminal offence — exactly the gap the bill targets. A virtually identical Hesse proposal failed two years earlier after leading legal scholars and practitioners objected on constitutional grounds. The deliberate timing of the first Bundesrat reading on May 8, the anniversary of Germany’s unconditional surrender, reinforces the legislation’s framing as a response to Germany’s specific historical responsibility toward Jewish life.

Why it matters: The bill tests a structural tension in German constitutional law: the Basic Law’s Article 5 protections for free expression permit restrictions only through “general laws,” meaning the state cannot restrict speech based on its content or viewpoint. Criminal laws against Holocaust denial passed the “general law” test because courts found they targeted a narrow, historically specific deception rather than a political opinion; it is much less clear whether “denial of Israel’s right to exist” satisfies the same standard, because the concept is inherently political and contested. The earlier Hesse bill failed for precisely this reason: leading constitutional scholars argued it constituted viewpoint discrimination — the state criminalizing one side of a political dispute rather than banning incitement or deception as such. If enacted, the law is almost certain to reach the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht), which would have to determine whether Germany’s heightened duty to protect Jewish life justifies content-based speech restrictions beyond Holocaust denial. The European Court of Human Rights has struck down analogous laws in other Council of Europe jurisdictions under Article 10, meaning a German statute of this kind would likely generate international litigation spanning both national and European courts simultaneously.

entry.title: Lebanon says Israeli strikes killed 39
entry.summary: Israeli airstrikes killed at least 39 people in southern Lebanon on May 9 — the deadliest single day since the three-week-old ceasefire was announced — with Hezbollah retaliating via drone strikes on northern Israel, exposing the agreement as effectively non-binding. (brief: full article unavailable)
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Israeli airstrikes killed at least 39 people in southern Lebanon on May 9 — the deadliest single day since the three-week-old ceasefire was announced — with Hezbollah retaliating via drone strikes on northern Israel, exposing the agreement as effectively non-binding.

(brief: full article unavailable) The strikes hit multiple towns across southern Lebanon including Saksakiyeh and Nabatieh, with raids also targeting a highway near Beirut outside Hezbollah’s traditional strongholds, according to Lebanese authorities. Under the ceasefire terms mediated by the United States, Israel retained an explicit right to act against “planned, imminent or ongoing attacks” — a carve-out broad enough that Israeli officials have used it to justify continued operations at roughly the same tempo as before the agreement was announced. Hezbollah confirmed it targeted Israeli troops in northern Israel with drones on at least two occasions on May 9 in direct response to the Israeli strikes. The escalation comes as the wider US-Iran war ceasefire in the Strait of Hormuz is also under strain; Lebanon is one of the fronts Tehran explicitly demands must be included in any comprehensive war-ending deal. The three-week pattern of “ceasefire” exchanges makes clear that neither party regards the current agreement as prohibiting offensive military operations.

Why it matters: The reported 39 deaths make the ceasefire in Lebanon functionally indistinguishable from low-intensity conflict, demonstrating that US-brokered agreements with broad defensive carve-outs offer little protection to civilian populations who cannot reliably assess whether strikes directed at them fall inside or outside those exceptions. The Lebanon front is directly entangled with the broader Iran-US war diplomacy: Tehran’s May 10 counterproposal explicitly demands the war end “on all fronts,” including Lebanon, while Washington’s proposal focused on the Strait of Hormuz and nuclear terms without addressing Hezbollah operations. That mismatch means any Iran-US deal that resolves the nuclear and Hormuz issues could leave Lebanon’s conflict legally unaddressed and militarily ongoing. International pressure for a more durable ceasefire is building, but the UN Security Council lacks enforcement mechanisms to compel compliance, and neither Israel nor Hezbollah faces immediate material incentives to observe terms that the current arrangement permits both to interpret at will. What to watch: whether the US uses its leverage in both the Iran war negotiations and direct diplomatic pressure on Israel to insist on a more enforceable ceasefire mechanism in Lebanon as a condition of any broader regional agreement.

entry.title: Once Again, Trump Looks To Get Out Of Paying E. Jean Carroll By Having The DOJ Substitute In For Himself
entry.summary: The Trump Justice Department filed a Supreme Court motion invoking the Westfall Act to substitute the federal government as defendant in the E. Jean Carroll defamation case — a maneuver three courts have already rejected — which would extinguish Carroll’s $88.3 million verdict if the Court accepts it.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Trump Justice Department filed a Supreme Court motion invoking the Westfall Act to substitute the federal government as defendant in the E. Jean Carroll defamation case — a maneuver three courts have already rejected — which would extinguish Carroll’s $88.3 million verdict if the Court accepts it.

Trump faces $88.3 million in combined judgments from two Carroll jury verdicts: one for sexual abuse and a separate defamation award arising from Trump’s public denials of Carroll’s account. The Westfall Act allows the federal government to substitute itself as defendant when a government employee has acted within the scope of official duties; if substituted, the case would be dismissed because citizens cannot sue the government for defamation in the same manner. Three separate courts have rejected this argument: the Attorney General explicitly declined Westfall certification during the original 2023 district court proceedings, and courts ruled that waiver belongs to the United States as an entity — not to individual administrations that can revisit it; the 2025 attempt came post-trial and post-verdict, violating the statute’s procedural timing requirements; and courts found that “denying you raped someone is not part of the president’s official job.” A Second Circuit judge described the litigation as “deeply burdensome” while refusing en banc review of the substitution question for the third time. The matter now reaches the Supreme Court, which granted Trump broad presidential immunity in its 2024 Trump v. United States ruling.

Why it matters: The 2024 Trump v. United States immunity decision created the legal environment in which this renewed Westfall argument becomes more plausible — the Court has demonstrated willingness to expand the scope of what constitutes official presidential conduct, and the same logic could theoretically extend to statements made during or about a president’s tenure. If the Court accepts the substitution, it would allow any president to escape personal civil liability by retrospectively invoking government immunity, extinguishing jury verdicts that have already been rendered after full trial. The procedural irregularity matters: the DOJ’s willingness to re-argue a question courts have ruled waived suggests the government is treating successive administrations as separate legal actors who can relitigate finalized procedural decisions — a theory with significant implications for civil litigation involving government officials. Carroll would be left with an uncollectible verdict despite prevailing twice before juries, setting a precedent that future presidential defendants could exploit to run out the clock on civil accountability. The case is now a direct test of whether the Court’s 2024 immunity expansion extends into civil defamation law, a domain where First Amendment doctrine has previously treated presidential speech about public controversies as a matter of free expression rather than sovereign immunity.

entry.title: What I learned attending all those Supreme Court oral arguments this term
entry.summary: SCOTUSblog’s Amy Howe attended nearly every oral argument in the 2025-26 term and found a court under visible internal strain, with sessions running nearly double their scheduled length, justices speaking simultaneously in “face-offs,” and public inter-justice conflicts spilling from courtroom into speeches and social media.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

SCOTUSblog’s Amy Howe attended nearly every oral argument in the 2025-26 term and found a court under visible internal strain, with sessions running nearly double their scheduled length, justices speaking simultaneously in “face-offs,” and public inter-justice conflicts spilling from courtroom into speeches and social media.

Oral arguments in the 2025-26 term have nearly doubled their scheduled duration, a trend Howe attributes to multiplying advocates, more complex cases, and justices reluctant to cede question time; Chief Justice Roberts has indicated he may revise the format this summer. Multiple justices now regularly speak simultaneously — Howe calls these “face-offs” — with junior justices expected by unwritten protocol to yield to senior colleagues, and Roberts occasionally intervening when overlap becomes unmanageable. Attending arguments in person revealed dynamics invisible through livestream audio: Justice Amy Coney Barrett physically waved off Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson’s attempted interruption, and President Trump’s attendance at the birthright citizenship argument — the first sitting president present at any oral argument — visibly changed the courtroom’s tone. Women comprised only 30 percent of arguing lawyers in 2025-26, barely improved from 28 percent in 2016-17, and just 27 percent of Solicitor General’s office advocates — a striking gap given that office’s role in launching Supreme Court bar careers. Justice Samuel Alito expressed concern that arguments “can go on and on and on,” and in April’s session only one non-government lawyer argued before the Court for the first time among non-government counsel.

Why it matters: The practical effect of longer arguments is not more information for the justices — who have already read full briefing — but rather heightened fatigue and diminished engagement during second arguments in the same session, a dynamic Howe documents explicitly as visible from the courtroom. The public inter-justice conflicts from April 2026 — Justice Sotomayor’s speech about Kavanaugh, Justice Jackson’s Yale lecture criticizing shadow-docket orders, Justice Thomas’s public response — are reflected in the in-person dynamics: a bench that visibly argues with itself and projects internal divisions that once would have stayed behind closed conference-room doors. The concentration of the Supreme Court bar — with nearly all non-government arguing slots held by repeat advocates — raises access-to-justice concerns, since success in the increasingly extended, contentious format requires a level of preparation and institutional knowledge available to only a small group of practitioners. A format revision this summer could significantly alter oral argument as a legal institution: reducing time limits, restricting interruptions, or changing advocate selection rules would affect not only courtroom experience but also the signals the Court sends about how much it values live advocacy versus written briefs. Any structural change would also affect how the inter-justice tensions currently playing out in speeches might instead express themselves within the argument itself.

entry.title: Musk v. Altman
entry.summary: The Musk v. Altman trial, in which Elon Musk seeks Sam Altman’s removal and demands OpenAI revert to its nonprofit structure, raises fundamental questions about whether charitable mission statements embedded in AI company charters create enforceable legal obligations that override subsequent commercial restructuring.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Musk v. Altman trial, in which Elon Musk seeks Sam Altman’s removal and demands OpenAI revert to its nonprofit structure, raises fundamental questions about whether charitable mission statements embedded in AI company charters create enforceable legal obligations that override subsequent commercial restructuring.

The trial centers on OpenAI’s conversion from a nonprofit to a capped-profit company and its subsequent plans for a full for-profit restructuring, which Musk alleges abandons the founding mission to develop AI “for the benefit of humanity.” Evidence introduced during the trial shows OpenAI had fallen from second to near-last among major AI companies on the 2025 Stanford Foundation Model Transparency Index; the company announced plans to introduce advertising into ChatGPT in January 2026 and disbanded its alignment team in February 2026 despite repeated lawsuits alleging premature model releases. Shivon Zilis — mother of Musk’s children and a former OpenAI board observer — testified that Musk had attempted to recruit Sam Altman to Tesla’s board before their falling-out, complicating Musk’s claim that his motives are purely mission-driven. The Verfassungsblog analysis by Teodora Groza, published May 8, argues the trial highlights a gap in European AI regulation: the EU AI Act sets technical safety requirements for AI systems but creates no enforceable governance standards for the AI organizations that build and deploy them. Groza identifies mandatory internal safety boards with independent experts, regulator-appointed observers embedded in AI organizations, and golden shares giving public authorities a direct governance stake as the structural instruments necessary to fill that gap.

Why it matters: The trial is the first judicial examination of whether a charitable mission embedded in a tech company’s founding documents creates legally binding constraints that override subsequent commercial restructuring decisions — a question with direct relevance to every AI company that has incorporated public-benefit language in its charter, safety commitments in its documentation, or mission-driven representations to regulators and investors. If a California court rules that OpenAI’s founding mission creates enforceable governance obligations, the precedent would affect not only OpenAI but every US benefit corporation and AI lab that has made comparable representations. From the EU’s perspective, the trial illustrates why the AI Act’s technical risk classification system is structurally insufficient: it can regulate what an AI system does technically, but it cannot govern who decides whether, when, and at what safety threshold that system is deployed commercially. Groza’s call for mandatory governance instruments — internal safety boards, regulator-appointed observers, golden shares — goes well beyond anything in current EU or US law, and it is unlikely to reach the EU’s AI Act implementing regulations before 2027 at the earliest. The case to watch after the verdict: whether any state attorney general intervenes to enforce charitable trust obligations against OpenAI’s restructuring, which is the most likely domestic enforcement mechanism even if Musk loses.

entry.title: Germany Doxes “UNKN,” Head of RU Ransomware Gangs REvil, GandCrab
entry.summary: Germany’s Federal Criminal Police publicly identified Russian national Daniil Shchukin, 31, as the operational leader behind both GandCrab and REvil ransomware gangs that extorted more than $2 billion from victims worldwide.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Germany’s Federal Criminal Police publicly identified Russian national Daniil Shchukin, 31, as the operational leader behind both GandCrab and REvil ransomware gangs that extorted more than $2 billion from victims worldwide.

Germany’s Bundeskriminalamt (BKA) publicly named Daniil Maksimovich Shchukin, a 31-year-old Russian national from Krasnodar, as the operational head of GandCrab and its successor REvil — two of the most destructive ransomware operations in history, on April 5, 2026. GandCrab emerged in January 2018 and extorted more than $2 billion before announcing a shutdown in May 2019; REvil launched shortly after as its successor, pivoting to “big-game hunting” and targeting organizations with annual revenues exceeding $100 million. Investigators used a combination of Russian crime forum records indexed by Intel 471, cryptocurrency wallet analysis tracing $317,000 in illicit proceeds, and facial recognition software matching Shchukin’s mugshot to a 2023 birthday photograph. An alleged co-conspirator, 43-year-old Anatoly Kravchuk, was also named. Together they are accused of at least 130 acts of computer sabotage and extortion between 2019 and 2021, extorting nearly €2 million directly while causing €35 million in total economic damage. The BKA assessed Shchukin is currently abroad — presumably in Russia — making near-term arrest unlikely.

Why it matters: The public identification is part of a broader Western strategy of “naming and shaming” Russian cybercriminals who operate with de facto state protection, using doxing itself as a deterrent when formal extradition is impossible. Germany’s April 5 action follows the U.S. Justice Department’s February 2023 cryptocurrency seizure filing that referenced Shchukin independently — meaning both Washington and Berlin traced the same individual through financial blockchain analysis, demonstrating the maturity of multinational cryptocurrency forensic cooperation. REvil’s July 2021 Kaseya attack, which affected up to 1,500 downstream businesses, remains one of the most economically destructive supply-chain ransomware events on record; the attribution creates legal exposure if either individual ever travels to a country with an extradition treaty. The FCC’s March 2026 decision to stop certifying non-US-made consumer routers reflects growing Western recognition that criminal groups like REvil have exploited vulnerable home and SOHO networking equipment at scale. If Russia eventually engages in substantive peace negotiations, named individuals like Shchukin become potential bargaining chips for Western counterparts seeking accountability.

entry.title: ‘Scattered Spider’ Member ‘Tylerb’ Pleads Guilty
entry.summary: Tyler Buchanan, 24, a British national known as “Tylerb,” pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy for his role in Scattered Spider, becoming the second member of the prolific English-speaking cybercrime gang convicted in the United States.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Tyler Buchanan, 24, a British national known as “Tylerb,” pleaded guilty to wire fraud conspiracy for his role in Scattered Spider, becoming the second member of the prolific English-speaking cybercrime gang convicted in the United States.

Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old from Dundee, Scotland, admitted guilt in U.S. federal court to wire fraud conspiracy and aggravated identity theft for orchestrating SMS phishing attacks that breached dozens of technology companies in summer 2022. Scattered Spider is an English-speaking cybercrime collective that operates through sophisticated social engineering — members impersonate corporate employees to manipulate IT help desks into resetting credentials and SIM-swapping phone numbers. The campaign Buchanan participated in targeted Twilio, LastPass, DoorDash, and Mailchimp, among others, harvesting credentials subsequently used to drain cryptocurrency from individual investors. Buchanan personally admitted to stealing at least $8 million in virtual currency. FBI investigators traced him through domain registrations logged from his UK internet address. After rival criminal groups threatened violence, he fled to Spain in February 2023; Spanish authorities arrested him in June 2024 attempting to board a flight to Italy. He faces a maximum of 22 years in prison, with sentencing scheduled for August 21, 2026.

Why it matters: Scattered Spider is significant as a Western, English-speaking criminal group that achieved enterprise-scale breaches through pure social engineering rather than sophisticated malware — exposing fundamental weaknesses in corporate identity verification and help-desk security that technical controls alone cannot address. Buchanan’s plea is the second successful U.S. prosecution of a Scattered Spider member, suggesting prosecutors are methodically working through the group’s suspected roster, several of whom are believed to reside in the US or UK. The 22-year maximum sentence includes aggravated identity theft, which carries mandatory minimums that stack with other charges — a deterrent signal that courts treat social engineering at scale as equivalent in severity to traditional fraud. The Twilio breach had downstream consequences for thousands of downstream customers, including two-factor authentication providers, meaning a single social engineering campaign propagated through the supply chain and undermined MFA at massive scale. Prosecutors’ ability to trace Buchanan through UK domain registration records also demonstrates that even internationally mobile threat actors leave recoverable digital trails, which should inform how other suspected Scattered Spider members assess their own risk.

entry.title: Russia Hacked Routers to Steal Microsoft Office Tokens
entry.summary: Russia’s GRU-linked Forest Blizzard hacked more than 18,000 routers at peak activity in December 2025, modifying DNS settings without installing malware to intercept Microsoft Office authentication tokens from government agencies worldwide — defeating multi-factor authentication by capturing session tokens after users had already authenticated.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Russia’s GRU-linked Forest Blizzard hacked more than 18,000 routers at peak activity in December 2025, modifying DNS settings without installing malware to intercept Microsoft Office authentication tokens from government agencies worldwide — defeating multi-factor authentication by capturing session tokens after users had already authenticated.

Forest Blizzard, the GRU military intelligence unit also known as APT28 or Fancy Bear, exploited known vulnerabilities in consumer-grade MikroTik and TP-Link routers to silently redirect DNS traffic through attacker-controlled servers — all without installing persistent malware on the compromised devices. The campaign targeted more than 200 organizations and 5,000 consumer devices, with peak activity in December 2025 affecting over 18,000 routers; primary victims included government ministries of foreign affairs, law enforcement agencies, and third-party email providers. By hijacking DNS settings, attackers could perform man-in-the-middle interception of OAuth authentication tokens even from users who had completed multi-factor authentication — effectively defeating MFA by capturing the session token rather than the password. Security researchers noted the approach was deliberately “old-school”: no malware on endpoints meant traditional endpoint detection and response tools were blind to the attack. The FCC announced on March 23, 2026, that it would cease certifying consumer-grade routers manufactured outside the United States, citing this class of national security threat.

Why it matters: The campaign reveals a fundamental gap in enterprise and government security: perimeter devices like consumer and SOHO routers are rarely monitored by security operations centers, rarely receive firmware updates, and are rarely included in threat detection frameworks — yet they sit directly in the path of all network traffic. By operating at the router layer, Forest Blizzard defeated MFA — the most commonly recommended organizational security control — without cracking any authentication system, simply by capturing tokens after successful authentication. This is a tactical evolution that shifts the attack surface from credential theft to session token interception, requiring different defensive responses including certificate pinning, encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT), and network-layer anomaly detection. The FCC’s decision to restrict non-US router certification is the first major regulatory response and is likely to face legal challenge from foreign manufacturers, but the campaign provides the clearest evidentiary basis yet for treating home routers as national security infrastructure. The 18,000-router peak infection count suggests the campaign infected routers well beyond the primary government targets, using compromised households as unwitting relay infrastructure — a supply-chain-style attack that amplifies reach without requiring additional compromises.

entry.title: When Justices Turn on Each Other
entry.summary: In an unusual cluster of public conflicts across three weeks in April 2026, Supreme Court justices criticized each other’s reasoning and character in speeches and writings, reflecting deep institutional tensions over emergency shadow-docket orders and the Trump administration’s aggressive use of executive power.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

In an unusual cluster of public conflicts across three weeks in April 2026, Supreme Court justices criticized each other’s reasoning and character in speeches and writings, reflecting deep institutional tensions over emergency shadow-docket orders and the Trump administration’s aggressive use of executive power.

Three separate incidents within an eight-day window in April 2026 crystallized growing public dysfunction at the Supreme Court. Justice Sonia Sotomayor criticized Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s solo concurrence in Noem v. Perdomo — an immigration enforcement case — during a University of Kansas Law School appearance on April 7, suggesting Kavanaugh lacked working-class empathy; she later issued a formal apology calling her remarks “inappropriate” and “hurtful.” Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, in a Yale Law School lecture on April 13, characterized approximately two dozen emergency docket orders favoring Trump administration positions as “scratch-paper musings” that “can seem oblivious and thus ring hollow,” directly targeting conservative colleagues’ reasoning. Justice Clarence Thomas responded on April 15 by lamenting that he had joined a court that no longer “dealt with differences as friends,” and criticizing colleagues who recast themselves as “institutionalists” or “thoughtful moderates.” Justice Elena Kagan separately warned that the emergency shadow docket was “never” designed to be used to circumvent established precedent such as Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935).

Why it matters: Public inter-justice disagreements of this intensity are historically rare and reflect genuine institutional stress, not mere judicial temperament. The structural root cause is the emergency shadow docket: it allows the court to issue consequential orders without full briefing or reasoned opinions, which strips dissenting justices of their normal vehicle for public disagreement — a written dissent — and forces them into speeches and media appearances instead. The volume of Trump administration emergency applications has made this a routine dynamic, with major executive-branch actions on firing agency heads, immigration enforcement, and foreign affairs being governed by shadow-docket orders that provide almost no precedent for lower courts to apply. Sotomayor’s apology is itself significant: she felt the institutional cost of being seen as attacking a colleague personally rather than legally, suggesting that even the most vocal critics recognize the reputational risk. The practical legal consequence is a court whose most important emergency decisions lack the reasoned analysis that would make them useful legal authority; what to watch is whether the court uses Noem v. Perdomo or a successor case to establish clearer emergency docket standards — the only structural fix available short of congressional action.

entry.title: Justices Poised to Protect Generics Manufacturers in Skinny-Label Patent Case
entry.summary: The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Hikma Pharmaceuticals USA v. Amarin Pharma on April 29 and appears ready to rule for the generic drug maker in a case that will determine whether generics companies face induced-infringement liability for pharmacist dispensing decisions — a ruling that could preserve or gut the 1984 skinny-label system that keeps generic drugs affordable.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments in Hikma Pharmaceuticals USA v. Amarin Pharma on April 29 and appears ready to rule for the generic drug maker in a case that will determine whether generics companies face induced-infringement liability for pharmacist dispensing decisions — a ruling that could preserve or gut the 1984 skinny-label system that keeps generic drugs affordable.

Hikma Pharmaceuticals USA v. Amarin Pharma, argued April 29, 2026, asks the Supreme Court whether a generic drug manufacturer can be held liable for induced patent infringement when pharmacists dispense its drug for off-label uses covered by the brand-name drug’s patent — uses deliberately omitted from the generic’s “skinny label” under federal law. The dispute centers on Vascepa, a cardiovascular fish-oil medication made by Amarin, and Hikma’s generic equivalent. Amarin argues that Hikma’s marketing of its product as a “generic version” of Vascepa — combined with publicly available data about Vascepa’s patented heart-disease use — amounts to inducing physicians and pharmacists to infringe its patent. The Hatch-Waxman Act of 1984 explicitly created the skinny-label mechanism to allow generic entry for non-patented uses of a drug while a brand manufacturer retains patents on other uses; Amarin’s theory would effectively nullify that mechanism by treating commercial context as inducement. The Federal Circuit ruled against Hikma in 2025, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari on January 16, 2026 — its first major patent case since 2023.

Why it matters: A ruling for Hikma would preserve the skinny-label pathway that keeps the generic drug market functioning: generics companies must be able to enter markets for non-patented uses without fear that pharmacists’ off-label dispensing will expose them to patent liability they have no ability to prevent. A ruling for Amarin would functionally block generic entry for any drug with an important patented use — dramatically extending effective market exclusivity and reversing exactly the outcome Hatch-Waxman was designed to prevent. The stakes are enormous: the FDA estimates generics account for over 90% of all U.S. prescriptions filled, and brand manufacturers have used induced-infringement theories to block generics in cancer, cardiovascular, and neurological drug markets. The Federal Circuit’s 2025 ruling against Hikma was already disrupting the generics industry by making it practically impossible to launch with skinny labels; a Supreme Court reversal would restore the pre-2025 status quo and create a clearer liability standard for the entire $150 billion generic pharmaceutical market. Justices across the ideological spectrum expressed skepticism of imposing liability for third-party conduct — a skepticism that tracks the court’s broader reluctance to expand secondary liability theories in patent law, and signals the ruling is likely to be decisive rather than narrowly tailored.

entry.title: The BMW and Mercedes Climate Cases: German Federal Court Rejects Combustion-Engine Bans
entry.summary: Germany’s Federal Court of Justice dismissed two landmark climate cases against BMW and Mercedes-Benz on March 23, rejecting demands that the automakers stop selling combustion-engine vehicles after 2030 and drawing a constitutional line between judicial and legislative authority over climate policy.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Germany’s Federal Court of Justice dismissed two landmark climate cases against BMW and Mercedes-Benz on March 23, rejecting demands that the automakers stop selling combustion-engine vehicles after 2030 and drawing a constitutional line between judicial and legislative authority over climate policy.

The German Bundesgerichtshof (BGH) dismissed suits brought by three private citizens who are also directors of the environmental advocacy group Deutsche Umwelthilfe (DUH), who sought a court-ordered ban on BMW’s and Mercedes-Benz’s global marketing of passenger cars with internal combustion engines after October 2030. The BGH’s dismissal rested on three distinct legal grounds. First, the court held that potential climate harms from greenhouse gas emissions could not be attributed to the defendant automakers under established German attribution principles: liability as an indirect “disturber” requires breach of specific duties of conduct and a normative delineation of spheres of responsibility — criteria that general emissions contributions do not satisfy. Second, the court rejected the “personal emissions budget” theory: Germany has a national carbon budget, but no individual company has ever been assigned a share of that budget, making it legally meaningless to claim BMW or Mercedes “exceeded” an allowance they never held. Third, the court held that deciding when combustion engines should be phased out is a political question belonging to elected legislators, not judges. Deutsche Umwelthilfe announced it is reviewing the ruling before deciding whether to pursue the Federal Constitutional Court.

Why it matters: The BGH ruling is among the most significant judicial statements on corporate climate liability in Europe, establishing doctrinal barriers that will constrain similar litigation across German-law jurisdictions and inform courts in France, Austria, and Switzerland where comparable cases are pending. The attribution holding directly rejects the legal theory that underpins cases like Milieudefensie v. Shell — the 2021 Dutch ruling requiring Shell to cut emissions by 45% — suggesting that if the same theory were applied to German automakers in a German court, it would fail. The political-question doctrine applied here is narrower than its U.S. equivalent but performs the same function: shielding legislative prerogatives from judicial override on contested policy questions. That said, the DUH’s potential appeal to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) is the key variable: Germany’s constitutional court issued a landmark 2021 climate ruling finding that inadequate climate protection can violate constitutional rights, and the question of whether that duty extends to individual corporations has not been resolved. If the Bundesverfassungsgericht takes the case, it could produce a ruling that either entrenches the BGH’s limits or breaks new constitutional ground on corporate climate duty.

entry.title: Putin Says He Thinks Ukraine Conflict ‘Coming to an End’
entry.summary: Vladimir Putin said on Victory Day, May 9, that Russia’s war on Ukraine is “coming to an end,” floating the possibility of meeting Zelensky in a third country after a peace treaty is finalized, as Russia and Ukraine began a Trump-brokered three-day ceasefire and exchanged 1,000 prisoners.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Vladimir Putin said on Victory Day, May 9, that Russia’s war on Ukraine is “coming to an end,” floating the possibility of meeting Zelensky in a third country after a peace treaty is finalized, as Russia and Ukraine began a Trump-brokered three-day ceasefire and exchanged 1,000 prisoners.

Putin made the remarks to reporters on May 9, 2026 — Victory Day — hours after presiding over a notably scaled-back military parade in Moscow’s Red Square, which analysts interpreted as reflecting operational strain on Russian forces. The statement coincided with a three-day ceasefire (May 9–11) announced by President Trump, during which Russia and Ukraine agreed to exchange 1,000 prisoners in the largest single-day swap of the war. Putin’s precise formulation — that a meeting with Zelenskyy is “possible, but only after a peace treaty aimed at a long-term historic perspective is finalised” — conditions dialogue on a concluded peace treaty rather than offering it as a path toward one. He did not describe any Russian territorial concessions, reaffirm Ukraine’s sovereignty, or specify what “long-term historic perspective” requires in practice. US forces carried out air strikes on Iranian oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this week despite the ceasefire, complicating the broader regional diplomatic picture in which Trump is simultaneously managing the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict.

Why it matters: Putin’s statement follows months of US-led pressure and reflects the diplomatic opening created by Trump’s engagement with Moscow — but the framing reveals the gap between the two sides’ actual positions. Ukraine and Western allies have demanded any settlement recognize territorial integrity under international law; Putin’s “long-term historic perspective” is a known euphemism for permanent Russian retention of occupied Ukrainian regions. The three-day ceasefire is the first mutually acknowledged pause of any duration in the conflict and establishes a precedent for temporary halts that could be extended — or that could collapse, as prior unilateral Russian ceasefires have. The prisoner exchange at 1,000 persons builds marginal trust without resolving core territorial disputes and follows established prisoner-swap frameworks from prior conflicts. What makes this moment different from prior Russian peace rhetoric is Trump’s simultaneous active involvement: if he can freeze the conflict temporarily to claim a foreign policy win before the 2026 midterm elections, there is political incentive to push harder. Watch whether the May 9–11 ceasefire holds past its deadline — extension would represent a genuine inflection point; collapse would signal that Putin’s words are tactical positioning rather than a genuine shift.

entry.title: Péter Magyar Sworn in as Hungary’s Prime Minister, Ending Orbán’s 16-Year Rule
entry.summary: Péter Magyar took his oath of office as Hungary’s prime minister on May 9, ending Viktor Orbán’s 16-year rule, after his centre-right Tisza party won 141 of 199 parliamentary seats in April’s election on a platform of democratic restoration and EU reengagement.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Péter Magyar took his oath of office as Hungary’s prime minister on May 9, ending Viktor Orbán’s 16-year rule, after his centre-right Tisza party won 141 of 199 parliamentary seats in April’s election on a platform of democratic restoration and EU reengagement.

Magyar, 45, was sworn in at Hungary’s parliament on the morning of May 9, 2026, with Orbán absent from the inaugural session — a pointed absence by a leader who governed Hungary as what critics called an “illiberal democracy” since 2010. The Tisza party’s 141-seat majority in the 199-seat parliament gives Magyar the constitutional capacity to reverse much of Orbán’s institutional reshaping without requiring coalition partners. The EU flag was reinstalled on the parliament building on the same day, absent for approximately 12 years. Magyar entered politics in 2024 after his divorce from Orbán’s justice minister, gaining national attention by releasing leaked recordings exposing alleged Orbán-era corruption; he rose rapidly through civil society organizing before founding the Tisza party. Hungary experienced prolonged economic stagnation under Orbán — declining real wages, high inflation, and a significant exodus of educated citizens to Western Europe — which energized Magyar’s change platform. He has vowed to restore judicial independence, electoral integrity, and media pluralism, and to clamp down on alleged corruption within the previous government.

Why it matters: Magyar’s election is the most significant democratic transition in Central Europe since the post-communist era and directly alters the EU’s internal political dynamics. Orbán’s Hungary was the most consistent disruptor of EU consensus — blocking Ukraine aid packages, delaying NATO enlargement votes, and maintaining close ties with Putin while the rest of the EU imposed sanctions. A pro-EU majority in Budapest removes the single most reliable veto player from EU Council decision-making and could unlock billions in EU cohesion and recovery funds that Brussels had withheld over rule-of-law concerns. The judicial and constitutional repairs Magyar has promised — restoring independence of courts, electoral commissioners, and public media regulators — will take years and face likely resistance from Orbán-era appointees with fixed-term mandates that cannot be immediately terminated. The EU will need to decide how quickly to restore suspended funds: too fast rewards change symbolically before institutional reform is measurably implemented; too slow creates political difficulties for Magyar’s domestic reform agenda. The precedent matters for other EU member states where democratic backsliding is ongoing — the Hungary case demonstrates that electoral accountability can displace entrenched illiberal governments even without EU enforcement action succeeding.

entry.title: UK Warship HMS Dragon Heads to Middle East for Potential Strait of Hormuz Mission
entry.summary: Britain deployed the Type-45 destroyer HMS Dragon to the Middle East on May 9 as part of a UK-France jointly led multinational pre-positioning for a future Strait of Hormuz escort mission — the world’s most consequential oil shipping lane, effectively blocked since Iran shuttered it on February 28, 2026.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Britain deployed the Type-45 destroyer HMS Dragon to the Middle East on May 9 as part of a UK-France jointly led multinational pre-positioning for a future Strait of Hormuz escort mission — the world’s most consequential oil shipping lane, effectively blocked since Iran shuttered it on February 28, 2026.

HMS Dragon, a Type-45 air-defense destroyer capable of intercepting guided missiles, was deployed from the Eastern Mediterranean — where it had been operating since March 2026 to help defend Cyprus after the US-Israel air campaign against Iran began — onward toward the Persian Gulf region. The UK Defense Ministry described the move as “prudent planning” ensuring Britain is “ready” to secure the strait “when conditions allow,” adding that the mission requires Iranian coordination and will not begin while active hostilities continue. France and Britain have been jointly developing a proposal to lay the groundwork for safe commercial transit through the strait once the situation stabilizes; more than a dozen countries have indicated willingness to participate in the coalition. The Strait of Hormuz has been blocked to commercial shipping since February 28, 2026, when Iran closed it in retaliation for US and Israeli strikes that also killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Approximately 20% of global oil supply and 25% of global liquefied natural gas transits the strait annually — its closure has driven energy prices significantly higher and complicated diplomatic efforts. US forces carried out air strikes on two empty Iranian oil tankers in the strait this week despite the Trump-brokered ceasefire.

Why it matters: The deployment signals that Western allies are planning for a post-ceasefire world in which Hormuz reopens under international naval escort — a framework that would require Iran’s at-minimum tacit acceptance and represents a significant expansion of the maritime security mission that the US-led coalition previously operated against Houthi attacks in the Red Sea. The requirement for Iranian coordination is the central variable: if the Trump ceasefire framework produces a durable halt in US-Iran hostilities, a multinational Hormuz escort mission becomes legally and operationally viable; if hostilities resume, HMS Dragon becomes a potential target rather than a peacekeeping asset. The UK’s commitment of a Type-45 — a premium air defense asset with no European equivalent — signals London’s intent to maintain a leading Middle East security role post-Brexit, distinct from EU defense frameworks. Reopening Hormuz would immediately reduce oil prices and ease global inflation, creating strong political incentives for both the Trump administration and European governments to press for ceasefire durability. Watch whether France, Germany, and Italy formally commit naval assets: their participation would constitute the most significant European military coalition since Libya in 2011 and would test NATO unity at a moment when Hungary’s transition has just removed the most reliable veto on Alliance decisions.
