entry.title: LLMs Corrupt Your Documents When You Delegate
entry.summary: A new DELEGATE-52 benchmark study of 19 frontier LLMs finds that Gemini, Claude, and GPT models corrupt an average of 25% of document content by the end of long agentic workflows, introducing silent errors that compound over time across 52 professional domains including coding, medical records, and music notation.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A new DELEGATE-52 benchmark study of 19 frontier LLMs finds that Gemini, Claude, and GPT models corrupt an average of 25% of document content by the end of long agentic workflows, introducing silent errors that compound over time across 52 professional domains including coding, medical records, and music notation.

The paper introduces DELEGATE-52, a benchmark covering 52 professional document domains, and evaluates 19 frontier LLMs including Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude 4.6 Opus, and GPT 5.4 on their ability to faithfully execute delegated document editing tasks without corrupting content. The key finding is that even top-performing models averaged 25% document content corruption by the end of long workflows. The failure mode is “sparse but severe”: models do not make frequent small mistakes but instead introduce occasional large errors — particularly difficult for users to detect because the surrounding content remains correct, and passive sampling of a document is unlikely to encounter the error. Larger documents, longer interaction chains, and the presence of distractor files all worsen performance. Notably, the study found that agentic tool use — giving models access to code execution, file systems, and browser capabilities — does not improve document integrity despite conventional assumptions that tool-augmented agents are more reliable. The research defines the core problem as a “trust deficit”: delegation requires the expectation that the LLM will faithfully execute the task without editorial substitution, and silent corruption violates that expectation in ways passive review cannot catch.

Why it matters: Agentic AI workflows — where LLMs receive multi-step document editing, summarization, and analysis tasks — are the central enterprise AI use case in 2026, and legal, medical, financial, and scientific documents modified through AI pipelines that silently corrupt 25% of content would generate significant liability for organizations relying on those outputs. The specific finding that tool use does not help is important for product and safety assumptions: many AI system designers assumed that code execution or retrieval capabilities would make outputs more accurate, but corruption appears upstream of tool access in the model’s text-generation behavior. The “sparse but severe” error pattern is particularly insidious from a quality-control standpoint: random sampling of an AI-edited document has low probability of encountering a sparse, severe mistake, while comprehensive review eliminates the efficiency rationale for AI delegation in the first place. For the AI safety research community, this maps onto sycophancy and instruction-following alignment challenges — models likely corrupt documents by making editorial substitutions they believe are improvements rather than deliberately diverging, suggesting the fix involves training on faithful reproduction objectives rather than helpfulness maximization. Organizations deploying AI for document workflows should implement automated diff-checking at every step and treat AI-edited documents as requiring human verification proportional to the stakes of the document type.

entry.title: What the EU AI Omnibus Deal Changes for the AI Act and What Lies Ahead
entry.summary: The EU Council and Parliament reached a provisional agreement on May 7 to amend the AI Act, delaying high-risk system compliance deadlines by over a year while adding a new ban on AI nudifier tools and broadening permissions to use sensitive personal data for bias detection.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The EU Council and Parliament reached a provisional agreement on May 7 to amend the AI Act, delaying high-risk system compliance deadlines by over a year while adding a new ban on AI nudifier tools and broadening permissions to use sensitive personal data for bias detection.

The Digital AI Omnibus package, finalized in early-morning negotiations in Brussels on May 7, 2026, extends the compliance deadline for standalone high-risk AI systems under Annex III — covering biometrics, law enforcement, border control, and critical infrastructure — from August 2, 2026 to December 2, 2027, a 16-month extension. AI systems embedded in regulated products such as medical devices, machinery, and toys receive an even longer runway until August 2, 2028. The deal reflects sustained lobbying by European industry groups backed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who personally pressed for broader industrial exemptions and secured France and Italy's backing; Parliament ultimately limited exemptions to the machinery sector. Parliament's right wing prioritized industry relief; the left wing traded concessions to secure the new nudifier ban, which prohibits AI tools generating realistic non-consensual nude images and takes effect December 2026 — directly responding to millions of deepfake cases linked to Grok. Transparency and AI-generated content watermarking obligations under Article 50 retain the August 2 deadline, though existing deployed systems receive grace periods. SME privileges were extended to small mid-cap companies, and a new EU-level regulatory sandbox was established to allow controlled testing of high-risk AI.

Why it matters: The 16-month extension for high-risk AI removes the most immediate compliance pressure from companies developing AI for healthcare, law enforcement, and critical infrastructure — the sectors where certification requirements generated the greatest industry pushback, with compliance cost estimates running to tens of millions of euros per system. The delay is a direct concession to competitiveness arguments that the original August 2026 deadline would disadvantage European companies against US and Chinese competitors operating under lighter AI regulation. The nudifier ban is the deal's meaningful civil society win: placing an affirmative prohibition directly in the AI Act rather than relying solely on the Digital Services Act and criminal law creates a new EU-level enforcement vector against platforms hosting or generating such content. The Data Omnibus — the companion regulation addressing GDPR simplification — remains outstanding and poses greater risks, as it would broaden personal data processing permissions for AI training. The provisional agreement must receive formal approval from EU member states and the European Parliament, with Ireland taking over the Council presidency on June 30, timing that will determine how quickly formal adoption proceeds — and whether the August 2 transparency deadline triggers first compliance actions before high-risk rules take effect.

entry.title: Court to DOGE: Asking ChatGPT 'Is This DEI?' Is Not Proper Legal Process and Also a First Amendment Violation
entry.summary: A federal judge issued a 143-page ruling on May 8 finding that DOGE staffers violated federal law and the First Amendment by terminating $163 million in National Endowment for the Humanities grants based solely on ChatGPT responses to 'Does this relate to DEI?' — without statutory authority, reasoned analysis, or any definition of the term they fed the chatbot.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

A federal judge issued a 143-page ruling on May 8 finding that DOGE staffers violated federal law and the First Amendment by terminating $163 million in National Endowment for the Humanities grants based solely on ChatGPT responses to 'Does this relate to DEI?' — without statutory authority, reasoned analysis, or any definition of the term they fed the chatbot.

DOGE staffers Justin Fox and Nate Cavanaugh, described as having minimal relevant experience, reviewed National Endowment for the Humanities grants by copy-pasting summaries into ChatGPT and asking 'Does the following relate at all to DEI?' Judge Colleen McMahon of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York found the process void on three independent grounds. First, DOGE lacked statutory authority: Congress vested termination power in the NEH Chairperson alone, and the staffers had usurped decision-making authority, drafting termination letters under the Chair's name and overriding his recommendations. Second, the process was arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act: Fox testified he never defined 'DEI' for the chatbot, and the resulting terminations flagged a study of ancient Jewish texts as DEI-related and rejected a human rights study documenting Uyghur persecution in China on the same grounds. Third, the terminations constituted viewpoint discrimination under the First Amendment: the government admitted it was eliminating grants promoting a disfavored ideology, and the court stated plainly that 'DEI is, of course, a viewpoint.' The case was brought by the American Council of Learned Societies.

Why it matters: The ruling articulates what may be the most precise judicial statement on DOGE's structural constitutional limits: executive-branch advisory bodies cannot exercise decision-making authority Congress never delegated to them, and AI-tool outputs cannot substitute for the reasoned analysis the APA requires. The First Amendment holding is significant because it applies to grant administration — an area courts sometimes treat as executive discretion — establishing that the government cannot condition NEH grants on viewpoint conformity. The arbitrary-and-capricious analysis creates a reproducible legal template: any federal agency whose decisions were influenced by DOGE staffers lacking statutory authority faces identical APA challenges, and the ChatGPT methodology makes those challenges especially easy to document through agency records requests. DOGE has terminated billions of dollars in grants across multiple agencies using similar review processes, and this ruling directly raises the viability of parallel suits challenging those terminations nationwide. The decision also opens a broader debate about government use of AI tools in regulatory and enforcement contexts — whether AI-assisted screening can ever satisfy the APA's requirement for reasoned decision-making, and what level of documentation such processes require to withstand judicial review.

entry.title: Eighth Circuit Kills FCC's Digital Discrimination Rule, Eliminating Federal Oversight of Racial Broadband Gaps
entry.summary: The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously vacated the Biden FCC's 2023 digital discrimination rule on May 8, holding the Commission exceeded its statutory authority by imposing disparate-impact liability on broadband providers — eliminating the only federal mechanism for addressing documented racial and economic gaps in internet infrastructure deployment.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously vacated the Biden FCC's 2023 digital discrimination rule on May 8, holding the Commission exceeded its statutory authority by imposing disparate-impact liability on broadband providers — eliminating the only federal mechanism for addressing documented racial and economic gaps in internet infrastructure deployment.

The FCC's 2023 digital discrimination rule, one of the final major Biden-era communications policy actions, created a complaint system under which consumers could challenge broadband deployment that produced racially or economically disparate outcomes, even without proving intentional discrimination. The rule applied not only to ISPs but also to their subcontractors and suppliers. A three-judge panel of the Eighth Circuit, composed of Republican-appointed judges, ruled unanimously that the FCC lacked authority to impose disparate-impact liability — the legal standard under which a facially neutral practice can violate anti-discrimination law if it produces disproportionately harmful outcomes without any showing of discriminatory intent. The court also struck the rule's extension to subcontractors as exceeding the agency's scope. FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, praised the ruling; consumer advocacy groups including Public Knowledge criticized it as leaving documented infrastructure gaps in low-income and minority communities without any legal remedy at the federal level.

Why it matters: The Eighth Circuit's ruling leaves intentional discrimination as the only actionable federal standard for broadband equity enforcement — a bar that the analysis notes 'almost never exists in writing,' making successful enforcement practically impossible. Research consistently documents that high-speed infrastructure is less likely to be deployed in predominantly Black, Hispanic, and low-income communities; the rule was designed to address this pattern through the same disparate-impact framework governing housing and employment discrimination. With the rule vacated, affected communities are left to pursue patchwork state-level remedies or antitrust claims, both of which face higher evidentiary thresholds and lack the FCC's nationwide jurisdiction. The ruling fits a broader pattern in which federal courts have used major-questions doctrine and nondelegation reasoning to constrain agency authority under Biden-era regulations — a trend that has affected the FTC, EPA, NLRB, and now the FCC in rapid succession. States like California and New York with their own broadband anti-discrimination rules are the primary remaining enforcement actors, but their jurisdictions are bounded and their resources far smaller than a federal regulator's, meaning systematic national enforcement gaps are now essentially permanent absent congressional action.

SpaceX agreed to grant Anthropic access to its 220,000-GPU Colossus 1 data center in Memphis, Tennessee — providing 300 megawatts of new compute capacity within one month — while Elon Musk simultaneously pursues his lawsuit against OpenAI, making SpaceX a direct compute backer of OpenAI's most capable competitor.

The deal gives Anthropic access to SpaceX's Colossus 1 facility in Memphis, housing more than 220,000 Nvidia processors with 300 megawatts of power capacity available within one month — enough electricity to power over 300,000 homes. Anthropic will use the compute to enhance Claude Pro and Claude Max assistants, and simultaneously announced it was doubling rate limits for paid plans, removing peak-hour usage caps, and increasing developer request volumes. The arrangement is strategically pointed: Musk is actively suing OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging OpenAI abandoned its nonprofit mission in favor of commercial interests, and SpaceX's simultaneous support of Anthropic — which competes directly with OpenAI — functions as a compute-level second front in that competitive conflict. Musk stated he approved the deal after meeting Anthropic's leadership, saying 'No one set off my evil detector.' Both parties expressed interest in eventually collaborating on 'multiple gigawatts of space-based orbital data centres,' tying the arrangement to SpaceX's broader IPO and orbital compute ambitions. Separately, Anthropic was excluded from a Pentagon classified-network AI deal that went to Microsoft, Google, and xAI.

Why it matters: Access to 220,000 Nvidia GPUs at a single facility is a training- and inference-scale resource that materially changes Anthropic's competitive position relative to OpenAI's Azure relationship and Google's TPU infrastructure, which had been the two dominant compute partnerships in frontier AI. The deal is partly a strategic Musk calculation: backing Anthropic with hardware while litigating against OpenAI functions as a market fragmentation move — Musk apparently prefers a frontier AI market with multiple competitive poles to one where OpenAI holds dominant position. For Anthropic, the benefit includes independence from sole reliance on Amazon Web Services as its primary compute partner, which reduces its negotiating constraints on pricing and priority access during peak demand. The orbital data center ambition is worth monitoring: if SpaceX's Starship-based orbital compute infrastructure materializes at gigawatt scale, it would give Anthropic access to compute outside terrestrial power grid constraints at a moment when US energy policy and data center permitting are becoming significant bottlenecks for frontier model training. The concurrent Pentagon exclusion creates a notable asymmetry in US AI policy: Anthropic, which has the most developed published safety frameworks among major frontier labs, holds no classified-network contracts, while competitors with fewer public safety commitments hold government AI relationships.

entry.title: Putin Denounces NATO at Scaled-Back Victory Day Parade Featuring North Korean Troops
entry.summary: Russia held its most scaled-back Victory Day parade in nearly two decades on May 9 — no tanks or heavy weapons appeared for the first time since 2004 — while Putin declared Russia is fighting an 'aggressive force armed by all of NATO' and North Korean troops marched in Red Square for the first time, publicly confirming a bilateral military partnership Moscow had previously downplayed.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Russia held its most scaled-back Victory Day parade in nearly two decades on May 9 — no tanks or heavy weapons appeared for the first time since 2004 — while Putin declared Russia is fighting an 'aggressive force armed by all of NATO' and North Korean troops marched in Red Square for the first time, publicly confirming a bilateral military partnership Moscow had previously downplayed.

The 45-minute parade in Moscow's Red Square stripped all heavy military hardware — tanks, missiles, and armored vehicles that are the traditional centerpiece of the annual World War II commemoration were absent for the first time since the early Putin years, replaced by a video screen displaying equipment deployed to Ukraine. Russian officials attributed the reduced format to the 'current operational situation' and Ukrainian drone attack threats; authorities restricted all mobile internet and SMS in Moscow during the event. In his speech, Putin described Russia's war in Ukraine as 'just' and said soldiers were confronting 'an aggressive force armed and supported by the entire NATO bloc' — framing the conflict as civilizational defense against Western aggression rather than a territorial dispute. North Korean soldiers marched in the parade for the first time, credited by Russian authorities with 'contributions in the Kursk region,' an open acknowledgment of the estimated 10,000–12,000 North Korean troops that reporting indicates fought alongside Russian forces. Foreign dignitaries present were limited to leaders from close Russian allies including Belarus, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Laos, Malaysia, and Slovakia. A US-brokered three-day ceasefire covering May 10–12 had been announced, which Russian officials cited as reducing the risk of Ukrainian drone strikes on Moscow.

Why it matters: The absence of heavy military hardware from Victory Day for the first time in nearly 20 years is a significant intelligence signal: frontline commitments are severe enough that Russia could not safely pull adequate numbers of tanks and armored vehicles back to Moscow for a parade without operational impact, revealing the depth of materiel attrition after three years of high-intensity warfare. The open display of North Korean troops represents a formal change in Russia's diplomatic posture — Moscow had previously minimized or denied North Korean military involvement despite extensive documentation, and marching them in a military parade forecloses further deniability and signals Russia considers the Pyongyang alliance a strategic asset worth advertising to domestic and international audiences. The NATO framing of Putin's speech — characterizing Ukrainian defenders as mere proxies of the entire Alliance — reinforces a diplomatic posture that complicates ceasefire negotiations: any settlement requires Putin to claim some form of victory against 'NATO,' not merely Ukraine, raising the political cost for Moscow of accepting terms short of its maximalist goals. The concurrent US-brokered Ukraine ceasefire window (May 10–12) is the immediate diplomatic test: whether both sides observe it will determine whether the ceasefire architecture can be expanded into a more durable framework or whether the conflict resumes full intensity after the commemorative period ends.

entry.title: Iran Accuses US of 'Reckless Military Adventure' as Hormuz Fire Exchange Strains Ceasefire
entry.summary: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the US on May 9 of choosing a 'reckless military adventure' over diplomacy after US forces disabled two Iranian oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, leaving ten Iranian sailors wounded and five missing — escalating a standoff that Trump insists still constitutes a ceasefire but which each side is accusing the other of violating.
entry.content:
📰 Read full article →

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused the US on May 9 of choosing a 'reckless military adventure' over diplomacy after US forces disabled two Iranian oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, leaving ten Iranian sailors wounded and five missing — escalating a standoff that Trump insists still constitutes a ceasefire but which each side is accusing the other of violating.

US forces fired on and disabled two Iranian oil tankers on May 8 after they allegedly attempted to bypass the American blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, leaving 10 sailors wounded and 5 missing according to Iranian state media. This followed a May 7 exchange of fire in which Iran fired missiles and drones at three US Navy destroyers transiting the strait — the US called the attacks 'unprovoked' and said it responded in self-defense, while Iran claimed the US had violated the ceasefire by targeting an Iranian tanker first. The month-old ceasefire framework, established after US military strikes on Iran in April 2026, calls for a halt to hostilities, reopening of the Strait, and a 15–20 day negotiation window to address nuclear issues, freedom of navigation, and sanctions; Pakistan is mediating the diplomatic talks. On May 6, President Trump had paused operations described as 'Project Freedom' citing 'great progress' toward a possible agreement, but subsequent strikes have continued. Trump has maintained the ceasefire is still in effect, calling the strikes 'just a love tap.' Foreign Minister Araghchi stated that Iran would 'never bow to pressure' and accused Washington of triggering military escalation 'every time a diplomatic solution is on the table.'

Why it matters: The Strait of Hormuz carries approximately 20% of global oil trade, and each exchange of fire carries escalation risk that could trigger supply disruption and oil price spikes — energy markets are already pricing in a conflict premium from the ongoing crisis. Araghchi's 'reckless military adventure' framing signals that Iran may be positioning itself to formally declare the ceasefire void, which would restore full belligerency and eliminate the diplomatic pathway currently under Pakistani mediation. The symmetrical accusation dynamic — each side firing while calling the other's action a ceasefire violation — mirrors the early escalation sequence that preceded the initial US-Iran exchanges in March 2026 and suggests the ceasefire architecture lacks a neutral monitoring mechanism capable of distinguishing defensive from offensive actions. Pakistan's mediating role is the critical off-ramp: Iran is reviewing a US proposal covering nuclear rollback, navigation rights, and sanctions relief, and Araghchi's public condemnation sets up domestic political cover for rejecting it without formal negotiating blame. The US decision to disable additional tankers while awaiting an Iranian diplomatic response is a coercive diplomacy tactic with historically poor outcomes — simultaneous military pressure and diplomatic negotiation typically hardens the target's domestic political constraints rather than accelerating concessions.
